title: US Closes Its Iraq Mission After 12 Years as Moscow Warns NATO It Would Use Nuclear Weapons If Kaliningrad Is Cut Off
subhead: The last American and British troops left Iraq on Wednesday, ending Operation Inherent Resolve and handing full security responsibility to Baghdad. Separately, Russia sent NATO a diplomatic note claiming the alliance is preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and warning of a nuclear response.

sections.heading: US Ends Its Iraq Mission, Leaving a Militia Problem Behind
sections.body:
The final US and UK troops left Iraq on Wednesday, closing the coalition mission known as Operation Inherent Resolve after more than a decade. About 100 British personnel departed Irbil in the Kurdistan region, coordinated with the US withdrawal under a 2022 agreement to pull foreign forces out by the end of September, according to the BBC. US Central Command confirmed the mission's end on September 30, and NPR reported Iraq marking what it calls a 'day of sovereignty'.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition mission marked Iraq's transition to full responsibility for its own security. Washington put a positive face on it: President Trump called it a 'decisive victory over ISIS' in a Truth Social post, and Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said responsibility for remaining security challenges now rests with Baghdad. Those challenges are the real story. A recent UN report assessed that ISIS is down to several hundred fighters capable only of unsophisticated operations, but Iraq's bigger problem is the array of Iran-aligned militias. Zaidi has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control, yet several powerful factions have resisted, and ABC News reported fresh Kurdish defence concerns about the emerging vacuum.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is leaving Iraq just as it is still at war with Iran next door. Tehran-backed militias in Iraq now face far weaker external pressure, which shifts the local balance of power toward the factions Zaidi has been unable to disarm.

sections.heading: Russia Threatens Nuclear Response Over Kaliningrad
sections.body:
Moscow sent NATO member states a diplomatic memo on Wednesday claiming it has 'information that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad', and warning it is prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Baltic exclave is cut off, according to Al Jazeera and the Associated Press. Kaliningrad is bordered by Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members, and hosts Russia's Baltic Fleet and nuclear-capable Iskander missiles.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte rejected the framing, saying the alliance is defensive, that Russia should 'stop the nuclear threats', and that Putin 'knows that he can never win' a direct escalation with NATO. The exchange lands amid a run of Baltic incidents: Poland has heightened its air defence after alleged airspace incursions, and Denmark reported a Russian warship firing flares near a Danish military helicopter earlier in September.
sections.whyItMatters: This is rhetoric, not a mobilisation, and NATO publicly downplayed it. But it shows Moscow is willing to put nuclear signalling on the table over a logistics corridor it depends on, raising the cost of any Western move in the Baltic. It also gives Russia a bargaining chip going into any Ukraine negotiations.

sections.heading: US-Iran Talks Stall as Rubio Expels Tehran's UN Delegation
sections.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his delegation to leave New York on Wednesday, ahead of schedule, after indirect negotiations stalled, Axios first reported and the Associated Press confirmed. TASS reported the White House had thought the New York talks might yield progress before it became clear they would not. The move came even as Iran said it had formally received a US proposal on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani saying the proposal was delivered to Tehran's Cabinet.

AP reported that mediators are still working to broker a deal as the conflict enters its eighth month, with major hurdles remaining. Both sides continue to claim control over the strait, and the war has inflicted heavy economic damage and battered Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington escalated diplomatically even while a proposal is on the table, a signal that the talks are close to collapse. If the ceasefire track fails, the Hormuz standoff and its economic spillover resume as the default condition.

sections.heading: Oil Slides as Hormuz Flows Recover, but the Recovery Is Fragile
sections.body:
Brent and WTI fell on Wednesday, with WTI touching a four-week low near $89 a barrel, as Middle East crude shipments neared pre-war levels. Saudi Arabia restored half the capacity of its East-West pipeline, pushing flows through the Strait of Hormuz up to 13.2 million barrels per day, according to FXStreet. The US also announced it would offer up to 40 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve in what Deutsche Bank described as the last drawdown of the coordinated global release announced earlier this year.

Crude prices remain volatile above $90 on some benchmarks because markets doubt the recovery holds without a lasting end to the war, given that both Tehran and Washington still claim full control of the waterway. OPEC+ is expected to keep November output quotas unchanged at its weekend meeting.
sections.whyItMatters: The oil market is pricing in a de-escalation that the diplomacy does not yet support. If the talks collapse, the recent price retreat reverses quickly, and the strategic reserve buffer is now nearly spent.

sections.heading: North Korea Warns of 'Merciless' Retaliation Over DMZ Mine Blast
sections.body:
Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, rejected Seoul's findings that the North planted mines that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone, calling the accusation a 'farce' staged by South Korea and warning of 'merciless' retaliation if South Korea opens live fire, according to KCNA statements carried by Yonhap and the Korea Herald. Experts cited by the Korea JoongAng Daily said the response appears designed to justify North Korea's ongoing fortification work inside the DMZ.

The incident follows the recent restoration of a South Korean guard post along the frontier, and Pyongyang's statement specifically threatened a South Korean army division on the western front.
sections.whyItMatters: The DMZ has been relatively quiet since the 2018 military accord lapsed, and a live-fire incident there could escalate fast with little warning. It also runs against Seoul's hopes of reviving inter-Korean dialogue under President Lee Jae Myung.

sections.heading: Seoul Commits $200 Billion to US Energy as Trump-Xi Chip Talks Change Nothing
sections.body:
President Trump unveiled the first three projects under South Korea's $200 billion investment commitment to the US, the Korea Herald reported: a six-gigawatt gas-fired power complex in Texas valued at $22.3 billion, a framework for eight large US nuclear reactors requiring separate approval each, and a review of Seoul's possible participation in the Alaska LNG project. The commitment sits inside a broader $350 billion package tied to last year's trade deal, under which Washington cut tariffs on most South Korean goods to 15 percent.

On the tech front, Taiwan's DigiTimes reported that the recent Trump-Xi summit left chip export policies unchanged, with Washington guarding its AI advantage while Beijing continues to pursue self-reliance. In Japan, China Daily reported that prominent Japanese figures are pressing Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to retract remarks that have strained ties with Beijing, while China urged Japan to adhere to its Three Non-Nuclear Principles after comments by Tokyo's defence chief.
sections.whyItMatters: The Korea deal binds Seoul's industrial base to US energy and supply-chain priorities, deepening the alliance's economic integration. The unchanged chip policy after the summit shows neither Washington nor Beijing is ready to trade away technological leverage, so the standoff persists.

bottomLine: Wednesday's main development was the US closing its 12-year Iraq mission, which removes a check on Iran-aligned militias in a country still adjacent to an active war. Russia's nuclear warning over Kaliningrad signalled that Moscow is willing to escalate rhetoric on NATO's northeastern flank, even as NATO publicly dismissed it. Diplomatically, the US-Iran track deteriorated as Rubio expelled Tehran's UN delegation, yet oil prices fell on recovering Hormuz flows and a final strategic reserve release; markets are betting on a de-escalation that the politics do not yet justify. Watch whether the stalled talks collapse outright, and whether Iraq's government can actually disarm the militias it now faces alone.
